## New cross-domain connections
- **[2026-11-26] The 11-12 entry proposed staging one Lightfin case as a live mystery for a few children. Matt Colville's first-session episode, ingested today, supplies the two rules that plan lacks: a fallback so the clue trail can't stall, and a way to get shy players talking.** [[lightfin/story-bible]] requires "a solvable mystery with a fair clue trail", but its only participation beat is the 15-second guess before the reveal, which never tests whether children can find a clue on their own. In [[podcasts/podcast-running-the-game-episode-2-your-first-session]] (10:17), players who think to check the smithy get to feel like detectives, and if nobody does, an NPC suggests it. That gives each clue a fallback, which matters most for the 5–8s that [[lightfin/adaptation-overview]] assumes only "guess along". Colville's other point (5:19) is that players find it easier to answer an NPC's direct question than to talk to each other, so the adult playing Sidney Stonefish or Blue Marlin in [[lightfin/ep-000-treasure-of-the-esperanza]] should open by asking each child something, not wait to be questioned. His "finish something in one session" rule matches the play-it-once ending the 11-12 entry took from N.D. Austin. **Smallest next step:** when Case 0's three clue stations are written, give each one a named fallback (who points the children to it, and when). Then log, for each age group, whether the children found the clue themselves or needed the prompt. That is the test of the 5–8 / 9–13 split.

## New investigation ideas
- **[2026-11-25] The three puts are valued by a model that ignores implied volatility, so the briefing can't see the signal Burry sold on. Real trade prices are free, and they put the NBIS put about 42% above its mark.** `options_pricing.py` says there is no live options source in the pipeline and uses about 80 trading days of realized volatility instead; NBIS is marked by hand at a fixed 80%. But yfinance returns daily bars for the exact contracts (pulled this run). Last trades on 11-24 against the marks in [[finance/trading-portfolio]]: NBIS $90 Jun-27 **$29.85 vs $21.00** (19 contracts traded), ORCL $120 Dec-18 **$15.80 vs $13.56** (578), PLTR $125 Mar-27 **$6.60 vs $7.08** (70). Together that is about €4,763 against €3,796, so net value would be about €967 (4%) higher. These are last trades, not bids: yfinance gave no usable bid or ask before the US open, and NBIS is thinly traded. The gap is not new for NBIS. The 80% input was below the market on every session since 10-01 (implied 82–97% in October, 116% on 11-24; my Black-Scholes, 4% rate, closes not time-matched). ORCL's implied volatility rose from 58% on 10-01 to 85%, while the model's input fell slightly, 65.2% on 11-16 to 63.0% on 11-24, through a crash. On 11-20, when [[finance/investor-letters/source-burry-trading-post-2026-11-20]] says Burry sold all SMH puts, three quarters of NVDA and half of NDX because volatility was so high, Fred's contracts closed at $31.00 (NBIS, 5.8 times cost), $21.90 (ORCL, 1.9 times) and $11.55 (PLTR, 1.4 times). ORCL and PLTR closed on 11-24 at $15.80 and $6.60. This refines two earlier entries: the 11-24 whipsaw idea used intrinsic value only ($18.81 for ORCL), and the 11-10 idea's step (a), filling in the Turso row so NBIS uses the same model, could swap a too-low 80% for NBIS's realized 128% (the 11-23 figure in the briefing), above the 116% the market implies. **Next step:** (1) check the real NBIS and ORCL bids before acting on the briefing's "lean towards taking it" (its ≈€1,130 net proceeds are based on $21.00); (2) mark each option from its own contract's last close (e.g. `NBIS270617P00090000`), with the model as fallback when there was no trade; (3) print implied volatility beside each mark, so the pending exit rule can include a volatility trigger as well as a price.

## New cross-domain connections
- **[2026-11-25] Learning's decision framework says to judge a choice by its odds, not its result. Fred's autobattler can measure exactly that after every fight, because its core can replay the same two boards under new seeds.** [[learning/framework-decision-making]] (AltMBA P3, from Annie Duke) says a good decision is one that "judged the odds well, even if you lost", and that successful people wrongly grade decisions by outcome. In life the other outcomes are never seen. In [[games/terrain-autobattler-combat-simulation]], dodge and crit on basic attacks are the MVP's only rolls, each fight is a pure function of boards, map, rules and seed, and a 16-unit fight targets under 5 ms. Two hundred re-runs of a finished fight should therefore take about a second. The new [[games/game-design-principles]] asks for a post-fight "why you lost" summary and treats luck as a choice between hiding it (Solomon's padded hit odds, [[podcasts/podcast-designer-notes-jake-solomon-parts-1-2]]), showing it, and moving it before the decision. This adds another option: keep the rolls and report their effect, for example "this placement wins 71% of replays; you drew a bad seed" or "you lost 88% of replays: change the board". It answers Solomon's complaint that you can play perfectly and still suffer catastrophe, and it fits a game with few lives, where one unlucky PvP loss costs a life. The same number is a design test: if nearly all boards win 0% or 100% of replays, crit is decoration and can be cut or made bonus-only; if many sit at 40–60%, luck is deciding lives. A keyword search of the game and simulation specs found no such feature. The [[games/terrain-autobattler-map-pipeline]] batch doesn't answer it either, since that compares factions across boards rather than one board across seeds. **First check, no UI needed:** take a few hundred AI fights from SimCli, re-run each 200 times with only the seed changed, and plot the win-rate distribution. Not run here. Leave out mirror boards, which are built to draw.
